Moving data

Sources & Sinks

A Source is pulled for Arrow batches until it says it has none left. A Sink takes one write per drain cycle, and closing it is the caller's job.

In one line
How rows get into a Dataset and back out again
You need
The saci-core/io feature for the traits, plus a connector crate for the transport and a transformer crate for the format
Read this if
Your Parquet file has an Int32 column where the component declares Int64, or your second run says write_batch called after finish

The shape of a drain cycle

Ingestion is pull: something calls next_batch() in a loop and appends each batch. Egress is push, where something hands the sink a batch and then finalises it. One constraint sits between them. A Dataset accepts a batch only when its schema matches the registered one exactly, so a cast usually has to happen first.

rows, batches, columns the registered schema

The two traits

Both live in saci-core behind its io feature. Every implementation lives in a connector crate that depends on them. Each is a schema, a step, and a way to signal done.

Rustcrates/saci-core/src/io/source.rs
#[async_trait]
pub trait Source: Send + Sync {
    /// Fixed per source instance. Must not change between calls.
    fn schema(&self) -> Arc<Schema>;

    /// Pull the next batch, or `None` at EOF.
    async fn next_batch(&mut self) -> Result<Option<RecordBatch>, SaciError>;

    /// Progress reporting only. Callers must not rely on accuracy.
    fn estimated_rows(&self) -> Option<usize> { None }

    /// Advisory hint: how many rows the caller wants next. May be ignored.
    fn request_batch_rows(&mut self, _rows: usize) {}
}
Rustcrates/saci-core/src/io/sink.rs
#[async_trait]
pub trait Sink: Send {
    /// May be called multiple times.
    async fn write_batch(&mut self, batch: &RecordBatch) -> Result<(), SaciError>;

    /// Flush and finalise. Exactly once, after the last batch.
    async fn finish(&mut self) -> Result<(), SaciError>;

    /// Batches must conform to this schema.
    fn schema(&self) -> Arc<Schema>;

    /// Backpressure probe. `None` if unsupported.
    fn pending_rows(&self) -> Option<usize> { None }
}

The bounds differ deliberately. Source is Send + Sync; Sink is only Send, because exclusive &mut self access already provides the synchronisation a writer needs. Concurrent writes to one sink are not a supported shape.

pending_rows has two consumers. Inside saci-service, the flow controller reads it directly off the runner's sink list on every pass, to back off when a sink's backlog grows. In a hand-built Scheduler, Pipeline::sink_pending_rows(component) surfaces it for a BackpressureSpec::Predicate closure to consult, though nothing in this repository calls it. Four built-in sinks implement it: ChannelSink (the row backlog of every batch still queued), PostgresSink (rows buffered but not yet copied), TursoSink (rows buffered but not yet flushed) and S3Sink (rows in the open object). A file sink has no meaningful queue depth.

request_batch_rows is the read-side counterpart, advisory in the other direction. A host tells the source what size it wants next, and a source may return fewer rows, more rows, or ignore the call entirely and stay correct, because the caller reshapes whatever comes back. Implementing it buys efficiency, never correctness. KafkaSource, NatsSource and PostgresSource act on it to size their own fetch. FileSource, HttpSource, S3Source, TcpIngestSource, SaciSource, TursoSource, ChannelSource and DataFusionSource keep the trait's no-op default and are still governed by whatever calls it.

Implementing a source is one method plus a schema:

Rustyield fixed-size chunks, then None
use std::sync::Arc;
use arrow_array::{Array, Float64Array, RecordBatch};
use arrow_schema::Schema;
use async_trait::async_trait;
use saci_core::SaciError;
use saci_core::io::Source;

struct RampSource {
    schema: Arc<Schema>,
    remaining: usize,
    chunk: usize,
}

#[async_trait]
impl Source for RampSource {
    fn schema(&self) -> Arc<Schema> {
        self.schema.clone()
    }

    async fn next_batch(&mut self) -> Result<Option<RecordBatch>, SaciError> {
        if self.remaining == 0 {
            return Ok(None);
        }
        let n = self.chunk.min(self.remaining);
        self.remaining -= n;

        let col: Arc<dyn Array> =
            Arc::new(Float64Array::from_iter_values((0..n).map(|i| i as f64)));
        RecordBatch::try_new(self.schema.clone(), vec![col])
            .map(Some)
            .map_err(|e| SaciError::generic(format!("RampSource: {e}")))
    }

    fn estimated_rows(&self) -> Option<usize> {
        Some(self.remaining)
    }
}

Emit the transport's natural unit rather than buffering up one giant batch when a source is driven directly against saci-core, with no host in the loop. The trait docs name no size: whatever a source produces is correct, because the caller reshapes it. Under saci-service, a source's own size matters less, because the standalone and stream runners size chunks themselves, admitting only what their adaptive flow controller currently targets and reshaping the rest with a zero-copy RecordBatch::slice. FileSource reads on a dedicated OS thread and hands batches over a tokio::sync::mpsc channel with capacity 4, so next_batch awaits instead of blocking the executor and the file is never fully materialised.

The batching contract

Two free functions do the driving. Note the argument order is not symmetric: the source comes first, the sink comes last.

Rustboth return the row count they moved
pub async fn drain_into_dataset<S: Source + ?Sized>(
    source: &mut S,
    dataset: &mut Dataset,
    component_name: &'static str,
) -> Result<usize, SaciError>;

pub async fn drain_dataset<K: Sink + ?Sized>(
    dataset: &Dataset,
    component_name: &'static str,
    sink: &mut K,
) -> Result<usize, SaciError>;
rows and batches who owns the loop

Three details matter. drain_dataset pulls the component's whole RecordBatch and issues a single write_batch, so a sink never sees the chunk boundaries the source produced. It returns Ok(0) without calling the sink at all when the component has no rows. And that batch is the raw one, so soft-deleted rows are still in it. Call compact() before draining to keep them out of the output file.

Rustdriving both ends by hand
use std::path::Path;
use std::sync::Arc;
use saci_connector_file::{FileSink, FileSource};
use saci_core::Component;
use saci_core::dataset::Dataset;
use saci_core::io::{Sink, drain_dataset, drain_into_dataset};
use saci_transformer_parquet::ParquetTransformer;

let mut data = Dataset::new();
data.register_component::<Trade>()?;

let parquet  = Arc::new(ParquetTransformer::new());
let mut src  = FileSource::open_async(Path::new("in.parquet"), parquet.clone(), None).await?;
let mut sink = FileSink::create_truncating(Path::new("out.parquet"), parquet, Trade::schema())?;

let rows_in = drain_into_dataset(&mut src, &mut data, "Trade").await?;
// ... run systems over `data` ...
let rows_out = drain_dataset(&data, "Trade", &mut sink).await?;
sink.finish().await?;

Or attach them to the pipeline and let it sequence the three phases for you:

Rustdrain sources, run systems, drain sinks, finish
let mut pipeline = Pipeline::builder("etl")
    .with::<Trade>()
    .with_source("Trade", src)
    .with_sink("Trade", sink)
    .with_parallel_system(ScaleSystem)
    .build();

pipeline.run_with_io().await?;
Sharp edge

run_with_io calls finish() on every registered sink at the end of every call. With a FileSink that makes it a one-shot API: the second call fails with FileSink: write_batch called after finish. For a long-running loop, drive the drains yourself. That is what run_standalone does, deferring finish() to the final iteration.

Sources are also drained one component at a time, each with its own row count. Two sources feeding two components with different numbers of rows will leave the Dataset inconsistent, because append_record_batch extends the shared row_count as it goes. Give every component the same number of rows per cycle, or drain only one.

Casting into the component schema

A component's schema is registered once and enforced on every append. The batch's schema().fields() must equal the registered fields(), compared by name, data type, nullability and order. There is no in-place retype of a registered column, so a cast is a pre-ingestion step. cast_batch is the pure function; CastingSource is that function wrapped as a Source.

RustCastOptions comes from the arrow-cast crate
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::path::Path;
use std::sync::Arc;
use arrow_cast::CastOptions;
use arrow_schema::DataType;
use saci_connector_file::FileSource;
use saci_core::io::{CastingSource, build_target_schema};
use saci_transformer_csv::CsvTransformer;

// The file says Int32 / Float32; the component declares Int64 / Float64.
let csv  = Arc::new(CsvTransformer::new(true));   // true: the file has a header row
let file = FileSource::open(Path::new("trades.csv"), csv, Some(file_schema.clone()))?;

let mut overrides = HashMap::new();
overrides.insert("id",    DataType::Int64);
overrides.insert("price", DataType::Float64);
let target = build_target_schema(&file_schema, &overrides);

let src = CastingSource::new(file, target, CastOptions::default());

The rules cast_batch follows, in the order it applies them:

  • It walks the target's fields and looks each one up in the batch by name, so column order in the incoming batch does not matter.
  • A column in the batch that the target does not name is dropped.
  • A column the target names that the batch does not have is an error: cast_batch: source batch missing column '<name>'. A cast cannot invent data.
  • A column whose type already matches is cloned, not converted. Arrow arrays are reference-counted, so a matching cast costs nothing.
  • The result is rebuilt against the target schema exactly, which is why nullability comes from the target and the output is append-ready by construction.

CastOptions::default() is safe: true: a value that cannot be represented in the target type becomes null rather than an error. Set safe: false to get the error instead. The two settings interact. If safe mode produces a null for a field the target declares non-nullable, the rebuild fails with cast_batch: RecordBatch rebuild error.

build_target_schema(source, overrides) covers the common case: clone a source schema and replace the data type of a named subset of fields, keeping every field's nullability as it was.

Constraint

A cast adapts types, never shape. If the component declares a column the file does not contain, no CastingSource configuration will help. Write a small wrapping Source that builds the missing array and re-assembles the batch. examples/connectors/scheduler_parquet_etl.rs does exactly that to pad a zero-filled output column.

What ships in the box

The traits, the two drain functions and the cast helpers live in saci-core. The factory contract lives in saci-connector. A connector crate carries bytes over one transport and a transformer crate turns bytes into batches, so a build pulls in parquet, arrow-csv or tokio-postgres only when it reads or writes that format.

A format key names the transformer that turns a connector's bytes into batches, and one crate implements each name. The transformers page has the schema rules and the options each one takes.

formatTransformerCrate
csv CsvTransformer saci-transformer-csv
ndjson NdjsonTransformer saci-transformer-ndjson
parquet ParquetTransformer saci-transformer-parquet
avro AvroTransformer saci-transformer-avro
arrow-ipc ArrowIpcTransformer saci-transformer-arrow-ipc

Every format reads and writes a file stream, and every format also carries discrete messages, so any of the five works on a TCP, Kafka or NATS node. Transformer::message_shape is what says how a batch splits into them: csv, ndjson and avro answer PerRow, one message per row, and arrow-ipc and parquet answer PerBatch, one message per batch. A message connector refuses its config at build time against a format that answers neither.

No connector resolves a format implicitly. A node that moves bytes names a declared transformer node by id, and that node's own format key is what the registry resolves. Which crates a build carries is one saci-service feature per crate, listed on Crates and features.

DataFusionSource has no factory, because it needs a live SessionContext, which a config file cannot express. Build it in Rust.

Every constructor, since they are not uniform:

Rustsignatures, not calls
// saci-connector-file. open_async moves the open and the metadata read off the executor.
// create appends to an existing file, create_truncating replaces it.
FileSource::open           (&Path, Arc<dyn Transformer>, Option<Arc<Schema>>) -> Result<Self>
FileSource::open_async     (&Path, Arc<dyn Transformer>, Option<Arc<Schema>>) -> Result<Self>
FileSink::create           (&Path, Arc<dyn Transformer>, Arc<Schema>)         -> Result<Self>
FileSink::create_truncating(&Path, Arc<dyn Transformer>, Arc<Schema>)         -> Result<Self>

// saci-connector-http. Neither makes a request: the source GETs and the sink
// sends on the first batch, so validate needs no reachable endpoint.
HttpSource::new(&str, Option<Arc<Schema>>, SchemaFrom, Arc<dyn Transformer>, Vec<(String, String)>, Duration) -> Result<Self>
HttpSink::new  (&str, Arc<Schema>, Arc<dyn Transformer>, method: &str, Vec<(String, String)>, Duration) -> Result<Self>

// The transformer each of those takes, one crate per format.
CsvTransformer::new(has_headers: bool)   -> Self   // csv
NdjsonTransformer::new(infer_max: usize) -> Self   // ndjson
ParquetTransformer::new()                -> Self   // parquet, Snappy
ArrowIpcTransformer::new()               -> Self   // arrow-ipc
AvroTransformer::new(compression: Option<CompressionCodec>, schema_id: Option<u32>) // avro

// saci-connector-channel. Returns the paired endpoint alongside the source or sink.
ChannelSource::new(Arc<Schema>, buffer: usize) -> (mpsc::Sender<RecordBatch>, Self)
ChannelSink::new  (Arc<Schema>, buffer: usize) -> (Self, mpsc::Receiver<RecordBatch>)

Only ndjson infers a schema, and only when schema_fields is absent: csv requires one, and parquet, avro and arrow-ipc reject one on a read, since the stream carries its own. FileSource and HttpSource report estimated_rows under parquet alone, summed from row-group metadata with no data read. NatsSource reports JetStream's own pending-message count in jetstream mode, and DataFusionSource reports whatever with_estimated_rows sets. CastingSource forwards whatever it wraps; every other source returns None.

finish() means different things per sink, and that matters when you decide where to call it. FileSink hands it to the transformer: parquet writes the footer and closes the writer, arrow-ipc writes the end-of-stream marker, and csv, ndjson and avro flush their buffered writer. After any of them a further write_batch is an error, and a second finish is a no-op. ChannelSink has nothing to flush.

The in-memory channel

ChannelSource and ChannelSink are a tokio mpsc pair dressed as IO. They exist for two jobs: testing a pipeline without touching the filesystem, and bridging a pipeline to another async task in the same process.

Rustthe sender and receiver are yours to hold
use saci_connector_channel::{ChannelSink, ChannelSource};
use saci_core::io::Source;

let (tx, mut src)   = ChannelSource::new(schema.clone(), 8);
let (mut sink, mut rx) = ChannelSink::new(schema.clone(), 8);

tx.send(batch).await.unwrap();
drop(tx);                                  // EOF: next_batch now returns Ok(None)

assert!(src.next_batch().await?.is_some());
assert!(src.next_batch().await?.is_none());

EOF is the sender being dropped, not a sentinel value, so a source you never drop the sender for will wait forever. ChannelSource validates each received batch against its declared schema and returns an error on mismatch, which makes it a useful place to catch a producer drifting from the component definition. ChannelSink clones each batch into the channel and reports pending_rows as the row backlog. That is the sum of the row counts of every batch still queued and not yet received, so the number reflects rows regardless of how large or small the batches are.

One caveat if you reach these through the config file. ChannelSourceFactory and ChannelSinkFactory resolve the halves through the host's channel registry, so neither hands the other endpoint back to you. The source takes the receiver, its paired sink the sender, and the source's EOF is that sink being dropped. A half whose counterpart never builds waits on a channel nothing will fill, which is why ServiceConfig::validate requires every channel name to pair exactly one ChannelSink with one ChannelSource. For real use, construct the channel yourself and pass the endpoint in programmatically.

SQL results as a Source

saci-connector-datafusion adds one adapter, in one direction: a DataFusion query becomes a SACI Source, streaming lazily so a filter or aggregation runs in DataFusion and only the result crosses into the Dataset. The constructors, the drain into a Dataset, and why it has no factory are on SQL results as a source.
